blocks.heading: Adar, the month of turning over

paragraphs.text: The Rav notes that the Megillah speaks of turning over twice: 'venahafoch' for the day of Purim, and 'the month that was turned over' for the whole month. If everything can be reversed in this month, a person too can turn himself around: one who did not daven or learn will start, and one who was angry will stop.

Tefillos are accepted especially from Adar to Sivan, so he urges davening for Klal Yisrael, surrounded by enemies. He adds the Gemara that one with a case against a gentile should pursue it in Adar, when a Jew's mazal is strong.

blocks.heading: Three days of preparation before Purim

paragraphs.text: The Rav goes through the Mishnah: villages once read the Megillah early so farmers could bring food to the cities, while today it is read on the fourteenth, and on the fifteenth in Yerushalayim, the one city surely walled since Yehoshua bin Nun.

He explains that the three days before Purim are like the days of preparation before Shavuos. At Sinai the Oral Torah was accepted under compulsion, but on Purim the Jews accepted it with love, so one must prepare to receive the Torah with joy.

blocks.heading: The kedushah of Keser all Purim day

paragraphs.text: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that the Megillah's holiness exceeds the Torah of Moshe, since it was accepted with love. On Shabbos the Keser kedushah of Musaf passes, but on Purim it stays all day, and no accuser can prosecute then.
'Yom Kippurim' means a day like Purim, and Reb Tzadok says Purim's time of favor is far greater. So Purim needs holiness and great joy, not a tense face.

blocks.heading: Purim is not a holiday of wildness; holy foods

paragraphs.text: The Rav rejects treating Purim like the gentiles' wild holiday. In a parable, a hen lays an egg that davens to reach a Jewish home, where it is cooked for Shabbos and eaten with onions; otherwise a gentile throws it on Halloween. Even an egg needs mazal.
Shabbos foods and Purim foods like hamantaschen, he says, hold great secrets and bring holiness into a person, so they must be eaten with kavanah.

blocks.heading: What one eats becomes part of him

paragraphs.text: A mitzvah creates an angel, but food becomes part of the person himself; this is why forbidden foods are so grave, since unlike other sins, they enter the body.
So each Yom Tov has its food: matzah on Pesach, dairy on Shavuos, the sukkah, holishkes on Simchas Torah, latkes, hamantaschen. Eaten with kavanah, the day's holiness stays with him.

blocks.heading: The Purim seudah and the danger of drunkenness

paragraphs.text: The seudah and the wine are obligations, from 'days of feasting and joy', but the Rav says drunkenness is not for this generation. The Satmar Rav wrote that most of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples drank only a glass of wine.

The Satmar Rav himself was an exception: at his twenty-minute tish he drank until carried out, then revealed Torah secrets he never spoke all year. Reb Avraham of Tchechanov measured a revi'is of wine. Following the Rema, brought by the Mishnah Berurah, one drinks a little and naps.
Drunkenness is a disgrace and a chillul Hashem, filling emergency rooms, so collectors should refuse wine. Adam and Noach drank, and what did it bring them?

blocks.heading: The open Megillah and its yeshuos

paragraphs.text: A Sefer Torah is kept covered, but the Megillah, holier per the Chasam Sofer, is opened fully, since 'Megillah' means revealing and its holiness must fill the world.

Every yeshuah is in the Megillah, the Rav says, as the Me'or Vashemesh writes: a king turned good, the wicked's downfall, and wealth for building, as Esther set Mordechai over Haman's house. So one wears Shabbos clothes on Purim.

blocks.heading: Why tzaddikim did not ask for the geulah

paragraphs.text: The Rav reads the king asking Esther 'what is your request' as Hashem asking Klal Yisrael on Purim. Why then did great tzaddikim not bring the geulah? He answers that on Purim they were shown that galus is not mere punishment but has tikkunim still to do.

Purim remains a time of favor when tzaddikim may do wonders. The Shomer Emunim once promised children for a ke'arah. He threw away a silver-plated copper one as falsehood, but blessed a man who brought a real silver one, and that man had a son and a daughter.
On Purim, he says, every Jew can enter the Holy of Holies. He closes urging early davening, charity and the day's mitzvos, and a blessing for next Purim in Yerushalayim.
